topic.title: Sanctuary cities
topic.proposition: Cities should limit their local police's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I get the instinct to keep federal and local law enforcement tightly aligned, but in my view, when local police act as an arm of federal immigration enforcement, immigrant communities stop trusting them. If someone fears that reporting a crime or acting as a witness could lead to a relative being deported, they stay silent, and that silence makes neighborhoods less safe for everyone, not just immigrants. Local police should focus on local crime, not double as immigration agents.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I understand the trust concern, but I think the greater risk is that limiting cooperation lets dangerous individuals slip through cracks in the system. Someone who commits a serious crime shouldn't avoid federal consequences just because a city decided to look the other way. Law enforcement works best when every level coordinates rather than competes, and treating local policing as separate from national enforcement priorities only fragments accountability without making anyone safer.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a fair concern about dangerous individuals slipping through, and I won't deny that coordination matters in serious cases. But I'd say the answer isn't blanket cooperation with every federal request; departments can honor detainers for serious offenses while still protecting routine interactions so people aren't afraid to call for help. Insisting on uniform federal alignment everywhere ignores that communities differ, and it risks making police into enforcement arms rather than trusted protectors in neighborhoods that need both safety and trust equally.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I agree that communities differ, but I think allowing each city to set its own rules creates an uneven system where someone's legal exposure depends entirely on which side of a city line they happen to live on, and that strikes me as an arbitrary way to run national immigration policy. Local accountability matters, but so does consistency, since enforcement priorities shouldn't shift with geography alone. This disagreement has clearly made its way into statehouses as well. This is the claim I am relying on. Between 22 and 33 states have passed laws banning or restricting sanctuary city policies
